piezas.titulo: Large Language Models: A Plain-Language Overview for Engineers
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2610.34585v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are neural networks trained on huge text collections to generate text by predicting what comes next. Engineers using ChatGPT and other generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools need a clear picture of what training changes and prompts add. The article starts with the Transformer, which connects words in context, and pre-training, where models learn to predict text. It then explains how fine-tuning adapts models to requests, with reinforcement learning from human feedback using human answer rankings. Next, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies documents, while chain-of-thought prompting encourages intermediate steps and agents use tools. FlashAttention lowers training and running costs by reducing data movement during attention; quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) saves fine-tuning memory. Readers get a life cycle figure and tables comparing methods and their limits. A short checklist for judging LLM evaluation claims flags test material in training (data contamination) and model-based grading (LLM-as-a-judge). It also covers very long inputs (long context) and hallucination, meaning false or unsupported claims. Check factual accuracy separately from whether an answer sounds helpful.

piezas.titulo: Secure and Functional Code Generation with Self-Evaluation
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2610.33450v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate functionally correct code that remains insecure. Security-focused fine-tuning can be expensive and is not always available, motivating inference-time approaches. Security-oriented prompting and retrieval can reduce vulnerabilities, but may also remove required behavior or apply defenses incompatible with the task. The challenge is to identify relevant security knowledge and use it to improve security without sacrificing functionality. We present SecGent, an inference-time framework that retrieves weakness context from the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) database and applies it to secure code generation. By connecting task specifications to relevant textual CWE records, SecGent provides task-specific security guidance without relying on retrieved vulnerable or patched code examples. Complementary functional and security tests check the resulting implementation, and their execution feedback guides repairs toward satisfying both objectives. We evaluate SecGent with four open-source LLMs and Claude Sonnet 5.5 across five programming languages on the CWEval benchmark. It achieves the highest joint functional--security success against four inference-time baselines for all five models. Across the open-weight models, mean functional-security@1 (FS@1) improves by 15.5% over RAG, with gains in both functionality and security, and by 19.8% over the strongest prompt optimizer compiled for each model. On Sonnet, FS@1 reaches 92.1%, outperforming the strongest baseline AutoGen by 4.8%. In a separate comparison, SecGent outperforms Claude Code with security-focused prompting by over 6% in FS@1. Feedback-guided repair further improves FS@1 by up to 6.7% over generation without feedback, primarily by recovering functionality while checking security.

piezas.titulo: PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2610.32101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit mode collapse, where their output distribution concentrates on familiar semantic modes. When diversity disappears, repeated sampling becomes semantic repetition rather than discovery, making rare but stronger solutions unlikely to surface and leaving self-evolution and continual learning difficult to sustain. Most remedies intervene only at inference time, shaping sam- ples without making diversity a model capability. We propose PRISM, a training-time framework that internalizes diversity within the model. PRISM combines (i) submodular curation that pairs each prompt with diverse-yet-correct multi-teacher solutions, and (ii) stochastic embedding modulation, which turns special-token perturbations into implicit signals for sampling distinct outputs. A theoretical analysis establishes the stability of this mechanism. On WritingPrompts and BookMIA, PRISM moves the quality-diversity frontier outward, achieving the best generation quality in all model-benchmark settings while maintaining the strongest or near-strongest semantic diversity across two open-weight model families. It also improves sampling efficiency on math and code benchmarks. Beyond inference, PRISM yields a stronger foundation for reinforcement learning, sustaining diverse rollouts and mitigating the diversity collapse commonly observed during RL training.

piezas.titulo: Contemporary diagnosis and management of vestibular migraine: a systematic review of conventional and CGRP-targeted therapies
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundVestibular migraine (VM) is a common cause of recurrent episodic vertigo, and it is associated with significant disability from recurrent vestibular and migraine symptoms. While there are a number of standard preventive treatments, their effectiveness is quite variable, and new treatments which target calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) have been identified as potential treatments. The purpose of this systematic review was to assess the state of the art in the diagnosis of vestibular migraine and to compare the efficacy of conventional pharmacological treatments with the new CGRP-targeted treatments.MethodsA systematic literature review was performed to find studies that assessed the diagnosis and pharmacological treatment of vestibular migraine. Randomized controlled trials, observational studies, comparative studies, retrospective analysis, cross-sectional studies, and case reports of patients with definite or probable vestibular migraine were included. Study characteristics, diagnostic methods, therapeutic interventions, clinical outcomes, and treatment efficacy were qualitatively extracted and synthesized.Results21 studies were included with a total of over 12,000 participants. The evidence comprised predominantly adult VM populations together with one large pediatric multicenter study. Among adult studies, participants were predominantly middle-aged women. The Bárány Society/ICHD criteria were used as a primary basis for the diagnostic evaluation, with selective tests of the vestibular system and neuroimaging to rule out alternative diagnoses. conventional preventive therapies were associated with reductions in vertigo frequency, headache burden, and dizziness-related disability. Anti-CGRP therapies including erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, rimegepant, and ubrogepant, were associated with clinically meaningful improvements in vertigo frequency, monthly dizziness days, disability scores, headache outcomes, and patient-reported quality of life.ConclusionA multimodal approach to the clinical evaluation of vestibular migraine is supported by current evidence, and both traditional preventive treatments and CGRP-targeted treatments have demonstrated benefit across vestibular and migraine-related outcomes. CGRP-targeted therapies represent a promising emerging therapeutic option, particularly for patients with persistent or refractory symptoms. however, the limited randomized evidence and scarcity of direct head-to-head comparisons with conventional therapies preclude firm conclusions regarding their comparative effectiveness. Systematic review registration: identifier: CRD420261427685.

destilado.texto: ¿Puede una nueva clase de fármacos aliviar los mareos de la migraña vestibular? Si se confirman estos resultados, los pacientes podrían preferir terapias CGRP sobre los preventivos tradicionales.

piezas.titulo: Somatotopic Organization of the Ventroposterior Nucleus of the Thalamus in Macaque Monkeys with Dorsal Spinal Cord Injuries Sustained During Early Postnatal Development
piezas.resumenOriginal: Injuries to peripheral nerves or the spinal cord lead to changes in the topographic organization in the brain at multiple levels along the sensory pathways. In adult monkeys large-scale deafferentations due to transection of the dorsal columns of the spinal cord at cervical levels result in large-scale reorganizations such that the deafferented neurons in the hand representation of somatosensory cortical area 3b start responding to anatomically distant body parts such as the chin. However, reorganization following dorsal column injuries depends upon the age at the time of the injury. The somatotopy of areas 3b, 1 and 2 in macaque monkeys with injuries sustained on or before postnatal day (PND) 5 is very normal-like. Whereas in monkeys with injuries sustained between PND9 and PND12, a large extent of the deafferented somatosensory cortex remains unresponsive to peripheral touch, with neurons at only a few sites responding to touch on the face or arm. Here we determined the organization of the ventroposterior nucleus (VPN) of the thalamus in four of these monkeys (Macaca radiata, 3 females, 1 male) that received lesions of the dorsal columns on PND 3, 5 and 9. We show that the nature of reorganization of VPN largely resembles that of the somatosensory cortex. Somatotopy is normal-like after lesions on PND3 and 5, whereas after lesion on PND9, the deprived neurons are largely unresponsive to peripheral touch, with a limited expansion of the chin representation.

piezas.titulo: Agent Factory recap: Agent harnesses, shifting left, and autonomous coding
piezas.resumenOriginal: In this episode of The Agent Factory , we explore the reality of building with autonomous agents alongside Ryan Lopopolo, a software engineer at Google Cloud and the person who coined the term agent harness . From throwing out manual code editors to treating team collaboration like leveling up RPG stats, Ryan breaks down how grounding models in rich context and shifting interventions left unlocks high levels of agent autonomy. This post guides you through the key ideas from our conversation. Use it to quickly recap topics or dive deeper into specific segments with links and timestamps. The Agent Harness - What is it? Timestamp: [ 00:30 ] An AI agent as we're defining it here is a large language model (LLM) plus an agent harness . Think of the harness as everything wrapped around the LLM that isn't the model itself. For example, if you're working in Google Antigravity using Gemini 3.8 Flash , Gemini Flash is the LLM and Google Antigravity is the harness. While an unassisted model can answer simple questions out of the box, it can't check live conditions or interact with your workspace on its own. When a user asks a question like "Why is the sky blue?" , an unassisted LLM can respond without issue. However, when asked a question like "Should I wear a raincoat today?" , the model can't answer on its own because it lacks the necessary data. The harness catches the intent, queries live weather tools, bundles that context back into the prompt, and hands it to the model to produce an informed answer. Ryan Lopopolo on agent harnesses and autonomous coding Tilde Thurium sat down with Ryan Lopopolo to discuss what it takes to run fully autonomous coding workflows in production. See the summary below! Coining the harness and writing zero production code Timestamp: [ 02:22 ] The term agent harness grew out of Ryan's extensive work on autonomous coding agents, culminating in a February 2026 essay on leveraging coding models in an agent-first world. Ryan shared that he hasn't opened a traditional code editor since May of last year, maintaining that streak through his transition into Google Cloud . In this paradigm, engineers no longer author or review individual lines of syntax; instead, they operate at the level of natural language specifications and inspect the final artifacts, such as pull requests, documents, and spreadsheets. Then they determine whether the end result meets organizational standards. Harness engineering is the study and the practice of putting a model into an environment where it can succeed. If you don't do that work, you end up doing what I call 'prompt and pray'. Ryan Lopopolo Context curation and lazy prompting Timestamp: [ 03:35 ] Upfront harness investment pays off by allowing engineers to become lazy prompters. When the repository contains structured documentation, clear interfaces, and discoverable tools, you do not need to paste walls of text into a prompt box every morning "I aspire to be an incredibly lazy prompter. If I have done the job to give the model the tools and context it needs to ground itself, I don't need to write a long prompt. It figures it out." The model uses its harness to pull relevant context, allowing it to navigate large codebases and execute complex tasks without oversight. Shifting left: engineering best practices as autonomous guardrails Timestamp: [ 05:00 ] When an agent fails, developers face a whole spectrum of interventions. The most common reflex is to fiddle with the prompt or retry, but that never scales across a team. "The simplest, smooth-brain, stupidest intervention I can think of is literally just: try my prompt again without changing anything else. But shifting left means moving interventions earlier into the development lifecycle where they are cheapest and automated: from prompts, to repo docs, to linters, to tests, and all the way to upstream evals." Instead of hoping the model guesses right on the next turn, shifting left embeds standards directly into the environment. Linters, tests, and AGENTS.md files act as durable memory and enforcement of what you think good looks like, making sure the agent stays on the rails without needing constant hand-holding. Leveraging established tools and determinism Timestamp: [ 06:50 ] Agents shine when they're handed tools that already mirror patterns heavily represented in pre-training data. Pairing models with standard command-line interfaces moves reasoning into determinism, shifting the burden of context aggregation away from the model and onto reliable tools. Ryan also shared an environmental design trick for context efficiency: structuring markdown files so link anchors sit directly beneath their corresponding prose blocks rather than inline. This prevents context clutter and mitigates "lost in the middle" retrieval issues. Because Ryan operates exclusively by reviewing end-state artifacts, keeping documentation readable allows him to easily inspect execution runs: "I want to be able to look at the pull request and review it. If it made a bad decision, I need to know where it went off the rails so I can whack the agent on the head and make sure it does not make that same mistake again." Long horizons and expanding the agentic loop Timestamp: [ 09:45 ] The central challenge of harness engineering is ensuring that agents cohere over long time horizons. Because human organizations produce software through iterative refinement rather than single-shot prompts, agent workflows must mirror that cadence. Harness engineering uses tightly scoped, reviewable pull requests to narrow the agent's state space. Stacking these high-confidence changes end-to-end allows supervisors to gradually expand the loop size, building trust until agents can autonomously execute large-scale initiatives, including entire language migrations Curating agent teams like RPG stats Timestamp: [ 11:58 ] Rather than divvying up sprint tasks based on individual specialties, having a diverse team contribute to an agent turns it into a central producer of work that carries everyone's strengths. Ryan compared leveling up an agent's capabilities to building out a character sheet: "[It's like] building out the stats of your RPG character. I get a new person on the team who is a React architect and boom! The attention that they pay is able to bump out the stats in front-end architecture and performance." With that collective expertise baked into the environment, the agent can autonomously classify incoming work and activate the exact skills it needs on demand, operating as both a backend architect and a front-end specialist. Accruing leverage in tools, not custom harnesses Timestamp: [ 14:38 ] For developers wondering whether to build their own custom agent harness, Ryan offered clear advice: don't build one from scratch. Standard harnesses already provide the foundational primitives: file reading, grep search, and command execution. Over-scaffolding an agent with rigid, bespoke frameworks creates technical debt and leads to sunk-cost traps when frontier models advance. "If you focus all of your efforts on improving quality on tools and context, you can freely adopt the newest models as they come out and you'll be constantly accruing leverage into a bit of the system that will never become obsolete." Operating Google Cloud and eliminating capability overhang Timestamp: [ 16:47 ] Discussing his work at Google Cloud , Ryan outlined his motivation to eliminate capability overhang : the delta between what frontier AI models are theoretically capable of and how much useful work is currently extracted in production. Because the cloud functions as a massive, programmable surface, equipping agents with direct interfaces to Google Cloud lets them manage and deploy infrastructure effectively, turning raw model capability into tangible enterprise utility. Continually updating your priors on AI Timestamp: [ 18:13 ] The speed of AI development requires engineers and teams to actively unlearn old limitations and constantly reassess what these models can achieve. " It's very important to continually be updating what you think is possible with these lovely tools that we have ," Ryan urged. What broke six months ago often runs effortlessly on today's frontier models. Rather than getting locked into rigid workflows, developers should build around the two highly extensible interfaces that will remain relevant across every model upgrade: tools and context. "Agents will always need context in order to do that last mile adaptation into what you think good is. And as you can continue to... shift it to the left, in terms of increasingly capable tools which act as a form of memory and enforcement of what you think good looks like, you'll continually be amazed as the models are able to do more and more interesting things for you over time." How To Build A Custom Harness Next, Billy Jacobson started us off by showing how developers can customize their own agent harnesses for specific tasks. Under the hood: Why build a custom harness? Timestamp: [ 19:44 ] Before jumping into code, Billy unpacked why developers should understand the mechanics of a harness rather than treating it like a black box. Recalling advice from an engineering mentor that "You can just use the framework, but a great engineer will really understand the framework" , Billy explained that building a harness yourself is the best way to debug what happens when an agent breaks. You can evaluate three core design decisions for every workflow: Looping : How many iterations should the agent run, and what conditions trigger an exit state? Tools : What specific tools should the agent access, and when and how should it invoke them? Memory : How important is conversational and operational memory, and when should it be retrieved or compacted? Linear Agent Harness: Deterministic Single-Pass Execution Timestamp: [ 21:34 ] Billy demonstrated a minimalist linear harness designed for deterministic workflows where looping is unnecessary. This pattern is ideal for targeted inspections, file transformations, or single-turn data analyses where you want a high level of determinism and need the agent to perform the exact same execution flow every single time. Closed-Loop Agent Harness: Iterative Test-Driven Repair Timestamp: [ 22:45 ] When tasks demand active bug fixing and refactoring, a closed-loop harness provides the iterative reasoning required to reach a verified resolution. In this demo, Billy showcased an agent that applies an automated code edit to address a failing requirement, and the harness executes the unit test suite against the updated codebase. If the tests fail, the runtime captures standard failure logs and detailed stack traces, feeding those error diagnostics directly back into the agent's working memory. The process repeats continuously until all unit tests pass, backed by a five-iteration ceiling to prevent infinite loops and runaway execution costs. Guardrail Harness with Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) Timestamp: [ 23:25 ] For developers who require custom behavior without rewriting core orchestration plumbing from scratch, Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) provides scaffolding with automated memory management and execution safeguards. Billy walked through an example that leverages ADK's native context compaction to summarize older conversational turns, preventing context window bloat during extended debugging runs. Custom interception hooks inspect and filter shell actions before execution, automatically stopping high-risk operations such as recursive file deletions, database drops, or unauthorized remote git pushes. This architecture gives teams fine-grained control over tool execution boundaries while avoiding the maintenance burden of bespoke harness frameworks. The 3-Layer Agent Dev Stack: Gemini 3.8 Flash, Google Antigravity, and Google Skills Timestamp: [ 25:27 ] Next up, Smitha Kolan broke down why coding agents do not always require heavier reasoning models, emphasizing that high performance stems from balancing the three layers of the agent stack: Model , Harness , and Knowledge . "Your coding agent doesn't need a smarter model. It needs a better stack: model, harness, and knowledge. When all three click into place, everything changes." She then walked through the three tools she's been loving recently, one for each layer of the stack. Layer 1 | Model | Gemini 3.8 Flash : High-frequency agentic loops run between 20 and 60 sequential hops per task (inspecting files, updating functions, and executing unit tests). Because latency and API costs compound across iterations, a lightweight, responsive model like Gemini 3.8 Flash makes real-time agent loops practical without running up a massive bill. Layer 2 | Harness | Google Antigravity with /boost : Default Antigravity handles standard navigation and component creation. On top of that, the /boost command spins up an orchestrator that coordinates specialized sub-agents in parallel and concludes with an independent audit pass before modifying files. Layer 3 | Knowledge | Google Skills Repository : With over 19,000 GitHub stars and 100+ curated domain packages across Google Cloud, Firebase, Flutter, and Maps, this harness-agnostic repository injects precise domain context on demand, preventing agents from guessing cloud configurations Your turn to build Building effective coding agents requires moving past the reflex of simply swapping in larger models. As Ryan Lopopolo's philosophy of harness engineering illustrates, true developer leverage is achieved by shifting best practices to the left and investing in rich tools, deterministic verifiers, and well-curated context that survive model upgrades. When combined with fast inference models, structured orchestration harnesses, and modular domain knowledge, agents evolve from conversational novelties into dependable, autonomous engineering partners. piezas.titulo: Cortical responses to lipread and text-based audiovisual stimuli in adults with and without dyslexia
piezas.resumenOriginal: Phonetic recalibration enables listeners to adjust their perception of ambiguous speech sounds based on visual contextual information. In line with a specific difficulty in forming letter-speech sound associations, adults with dyslexia have been found to show no text-based, but intact lipread-based, recalibration. The underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear however. This fMRI study examined cortical responses during text-based and lipread-based phonetic recalibration in 34 adults (18 with dyslexia, 16 typical readers). Participants were exposed to ambiguous speech sounds /a?a/ paired with disambiguating visual information (“aba”/“ada” text or lipread videos), followed by auditory-only categorization trials. Contrary to previous findings, both groups showed robust text-based and lipread-based behavioral recalibration effects, with no significant group differences between typical and dyslexic readers. Neuroimaging data did yield group differences in the underlying cortical activation. Most notably, dyslexic readers demonstrated increased bilateral fusiform activation compared to typical readers during exposure to lipread videos and ambiguous speech sounds, with left fusiform activation specifically correlating with increased phonological processing difficulties. Additionally, typical readers exhibited higher right frontal activation during text-based audiovisual stimuli. These findings suggest that while adults with dyslexia did not differ significantly from typical readers in behavioral recalibration effects, they employed different neural processing strategies. Unexpectedly, this was particularly the case for lipread audiovisual stimuli. The relatively increased fusiform and superior temporal activation to lipread audiovisual stimuli in dyslexic readers possibly relates to subtle difficulties in phonological processing of ambiguous speech signals.

piezas.titulo: Fragments: October 21
piezas.resumenOriginal: Gergely Orosz is frustrated at those that entered his explicitly “No AI” essay competition and used AI. He goes on to say: When I start to suspect some part is AI about someone I don’t know: how can I tell how much of it is? And how much time and effort do I want to invest to figure out? I fear most people do not realize this last part: that when it takes time and effort from others to figure out what % is AI, and what % is YOU, then I will simply assume it’s probably 100% AI and 0% you So when producing anything that is meant for other humans, if you use even a little AI, you risk the assumption that it is all AI and pointless to pay attention to In general, I agree with him, and react much the same. Once I hear LLM Voice, I flip the bozo bit and check out of the post. But as I do this I have caveats. How accurate is my neural net at AI-detection, are humans taking on AI-ish elements in their normal communication? And more seriously there are some valid uses for AI. Jim Highsmith’s story of his second brain helping him deal with Parkinson’s is one. Another is folks who don’t know English well, using AI to translate. Am I being unfair when I flip the AI voice bit when I read/listen to them? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I was sad to hear that the Grace Hopper Celebration is canceled this year. It’s an event run by Anitab.org to promote women and non-binary technologists in the software industry. Many of my colleagues have been encouraged and inspired by going to this event, which makes a refreshing change to what is often a male-dominated world. It seems the current crusade against diversity initiatives has had a big impact on funding. We are still a long way from where we should be on gender diversity in our profession, and losing an event like this only makes things more difficult. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code . Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut. In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation: Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts. One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed. She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data. Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier. The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug. The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments. With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses. The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution. Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies. This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans. A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent Agents’ ability to consume lots of raw data also affects how we build systems. More logging gives agents more data to chew on. And thus far, the human is still necessary to direct the agent In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to While it’s a long post, it’s engagingly written and full of useful details. I hope my little summary encourages you to give it the read it deserves.

piezas.titulo: Comparative effects of different magnetic stimulation modalities on upper limb motor function and activities of daily living in patients with stroke: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
piezas.resumenOriginal: ObjectiveTo systematically evaluate the effects of different magnetic stimulation (MS) modalities on upper limb motor function and activities of daily living (ADL) in patients with stroke through a network meta-analysis.MethodsEmbase, Web of Science, PubMed, Wanfang, VIP, and CNKI were searched from inception to January 2026 for randomized controlled trials evaluating MS interventions for upper limb motor function and activities of daily living (ADL) in patients with stroke. A frequentist network meta-analysis was performed using standardized mean difference (SMD) with 95% confidence interval (CI). The surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) was used to estimate the relative ranking probabilities of interventions. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE.ResultsA total of 48 randomized controlled trials were included. For upper limb motor function, rPMS (SMD = 0.65, 95% CI: 0.19 to 1.12), rTMS (SMD = 0.96, 95% CI: 0.68 to 1.24), and combined MS (SMD = 1.01, 95% CI: 0.47 to 1.55) were all superior to conventional rehabilitation. SUCRA rankings suggested that combined MS ranked highest, followed by rTMS. However, pairwise comparisons among active magnetic stimulation interventions did not reach statistical significance. For ADL, rPMS (SMD = 0.60, 95% CI: 0.26 to 0.95), rTMS (SMD = 0.76, 95% CI: 0.56 to 0.97), and combined MS (SMD = 1.27, 95% CI: 0.94 to 1.59) significantly improved ADL compared with conventional rehabilitation. Combined MS was also superior to rPMS and rTMS alone. Sensitivity analysis excluding studies that reported only the Barthel Index showed broadly consistent results. No clear evidence of publication bias or small-study effects was detected. The certainty of evidence was rated as low.ConclusionMS interventions may improve upper limb motor function and ADL in patients with stroke. Combined MS and rTMS showed relatively high ranking probabilities for upper limb motor recovery, whereas combined MS showed the highest ranking probability for ADL improvement. Given the heterogeneity among included studies, non-significant differences in some direct comparisons, and low certainty of evidence, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and confirmed by high-quality head-to-head trials.Systematic review registrationhttps://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261302905, Identifier: CRD420261302905.

piezas.titulo: Heavy-tailed connections support robust neural communication
piezas.resumenOriginal: In the synaptic wiring between neurons, some rare connections are orders of magnitude stronger than most. This heavy-tailed connectivity is ubiquitous across different species, brain regions, and cell types, suggesting that it serves a general purpose for neural function. Here, we show, both analytically and in simulations, that heavy-tailed connections reduce communication errors in the presence of synaptic noise. In minimal models of individual neurons, noisy connections induce errors at a rate that depends only on a simple network statistic, which we refer to as robustness. For a fixed number of incoming synapses, neurons with broader distributions of connection strength are more robust and, therefore, admit fewer errors. Across several connectomes, we find that real neurons are consistently more robust than comparable null networks. In the whole brain of the fruit fly Drosophila, robustness increases with distance from the sensory periphery, such that central neurons are more robust than those involved in sensory processing. Together, these results indicate that heavy-tailed connections may arise universally to fortify the brain against noise in communication.

piezas.titulo: Prefrontal cortical morphometric covariance and cognitive task performance in healthy young adults: an exploratory analysis of Human Connectome Project data
piezas.resumenOriginal: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is implicated in many cognitive tasks, including working memory, reward-based decision-making, executive control, and metacognition. This exploratory analysis investigated whether individual expression of PFC cortical thickness and surface area covariance components is associated with cognitive task performance. The sample comprised Human Connectome Project (HCP) MRI data from 743 healthy adults (age 22–36+). Oblimin-rotated principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to residualized thickness and surface area for 22 PFC regions, controlling for age, sex, and ICV. Component scores were entered as predictors in separate regression models for the Flanker Age-Adjusted Score (inhibitory control), the Gambling RT Difference (RT for the same “larger” guess in reward minus punishment blocks), and 2-Back median RT (working memory speed). Parallel analysis favored two thickness components; a prespecified three-component solution (Global/Lateral PFC, RC1; Orbitofrontal, RC2; Anterior Cingulate, RC3; 53.7% of variance) was retained by decision, and RC1 and RC2 were only moderately stable across bootstrap resamples. RC1 was nominally associated with lower Flanker scores (β = −0.103, p = 0.027), opposite to the predicted direction, and RC2 with a smaller Gambling RT Difference (β = −0.103, p = 0.025); neither survived false discovery rate (FDR) correction (q = 0.054). In uncorrected models added at review, whole-cortex mean thickness alone robustly predicted Flanker scores but not the Gambling RT Difference; neither component association survived regressing mean thickness out before PCA. In surface area analyses, greater orbitofrontal surface area (AC2) was associated with faster 2-Back RT (β = −0.125, p = 0.003; q = 0.032 across 12 surface area tests and 0.064 across all 24 component tests), not explained by a speed-accuracy tradeoff. This unpredicted association persisted in most sensitivity analyses but was attenuated and non-significant when total surface area was regressed out before PCA (β = −0.065, p = 0.078). In conclusion, no prefrontal-specific association was robust. Global cortical thickness accounts for the Flanker association more parsimoniously, the Gambling RT Difference association was not robust under either account, and the orbitofrontal surface area association could not be separated from global surface area; all associations require replication.

No longer can engineers evaluate systems statically; they must master joint hardware design and network-algorithm co-optimization to navigate the critical trade‑offs between throughput, latency, and operational efficiency. The avatars represent engineers tackling the same problems from various perspectives based on their different roles. The simulated storytelling and dialogues make advanced engineering concepts approachable without sacrificing depth or interactivity, because the user is occasionally challenged to decide the correct answer that leads to the best course of action. A hardware engineer might push back against a systems engineer’s demands, for example, revealing the friction between physical constraints and algorithmic ambition. A computational validation specialist might interrogate a chip performance engineer’s optimism, exposing the gap between theoretical throughput and real‑world behavior. piezas.resumenOriginal: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum STAR Admin Thu, 06/15/2017 - 14:07 STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) and T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades) are two Colorado nonprofits who have partnered to create a series of respite camps serving adolescents who have autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Developmental Pathways has awarded the organizations a $25,000 grant to fund three F.U.S.E. (Fostering Unlimited Success and Empowerment) camps through 2018. STAR Institute offers premier treatment for SPD and brings expertise in social skills while T.AC.T. teaches trade and life skills to individuals with ASD and SPD with an emphasis on fostering independence and personal growth. “This is a very rare and exciting way to see two nonprofits interact. Our partnership to create F.U.S.E. allows both of our organizations to combine expertise in a way that best serves these adolescents to find new interests and gain the soft skills to successfully participate in peer groups and future workplaces”, says Dick Layton, Director of STAR Institute for SPD. The respite camps will be week-long day camps that host six students per camp ages 12-15 who have autism spectrum disorder. The camps will teach pre-vocational and vocational skills in a supportive, social, and inclusionary environment. Each camp has a different project for participants including: building a non-motorized go-cart with a partner, building an instrument to play in a band, and crafting board games. “The intended focus of F.U.S.E. is not just about offering a respite program for families. By generating new experiences for these adolescents, we hope to foster new skills, new interests, develop social skills, and give them a sense of empowerment to participate in what hopefully becomes a new hobby or future career interest”, says Danny Combs co-founder and president of T.A.C.T. SPD is a neurological disorder that disrupts the way an individual processes and responds to sensations. The disorder can affect people in only one sense–for example, just touch or just sight or just movement–or in multiple senses. One person with SPD may over-respond to touch sensation and find clothing, physical contact, other tactile sensory input to be unbearable and/or they may respond to visual or auditory or another sensory input. Another person might under-respond and show little or no reaction to stimulation, even pain or extreme hot and cold or just may be slow to respond to sensation. SPD and ASD have a high co-morbidity rate, but are also found to be standalone disorders. ASD refers to conditions categorized by challenges with social skills, repetitive behaviors, speech and nonverbal communication, as well as by unique strengths and differences that can occur on a range from mild to severe. Individuals with ASD and SPD frequently struggle with interpersonal skills over their lifetime and are often underestimated, which can lead to specific difficulty in career and relationships. F.U.S.E. aims to give individuals the ability to ignite new interests and feel empowered in group collaboration, which can lead to greater success in career and relationships. piezas.titulo: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation targeting motor cortical region induces cell-type-specific transcriptional reprogramming and behavioral recovery in non-human primate model of Rett syndrome
piezas.resumenOriginal: Rett syndrome (RTT), a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by mutations in the MECP2 gene, currently lacks effective treatments. The motor cortex is a pivotal hub in RTT and autism spectrum disorders, and its impairments contribute to motor, social, and cognitive deficits. Here we examined the effects of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) targeting motor area in non-human primate of RTT (MECP2-mutant monkey) and investigated neuromolecular basis underlying therapeutic effects. We identified a new treatment target, ventral premotor cortex (PMv), for RTT and found that following a 20-day rTMS course, several behavioral and functional connectivity measures showed directional changes. Neuroimaging analyses confirmed that rTMS induced reorganization of large-scale functional connectivity with enhanced functional integration between the somatomotor and the salience networks and normalized coupling between the motor cortex and both the thalamus and the anterior cingulate cortex. Notably, single-nucleus RNA sequencing revealed that rTMS triggered cell-type-specific transcriptional reprogramming: it rescued pathological hyperactivity of excitatory neurons by restoring the expression and regulatory networks of immediate early genes (e.g., FOS, EGR1) and corrected dysregulated intercellular signaling (e.g., NRG, WNT). These findings indicate that targeting motor cortical areas with brain stimulation may treat RTT, which warrants further clinical validation.

piezas.titulo: Functional recovery and domain-specific quality of life after moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury: a mixed-effects analysis
piezas.resumenOriginal: IntroductionThe purpose of this study is to investigate how functional recovery, measured by the Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended (GOSE), is associated with quality of life (QOL) as measured by the Quality of Life after Brain Injury (QOLIBRI) survey in adults with moderate-to-severe TBI (msTBI). We aim to better understand this nuanced relationship to guide more individualized and effective rehabilitation planning.MethodsThis study enrolled 138 adults aged 18 to 65 years with a history of msTBI one-year post-injury. Functional recovery was assessed using the GOSE score, administered face-to-face by a single trained investigator. Health-related QOL was evaluated using the QOLIBRI across six domains: Emotion, Feeling, Independence, Physical, Social, and Thinking. A mixed effects model using participant as the primary random effect and estimated marginal trends were calculated to examine the relationship between GOSE scores and QOLIBRI outcomes.ResultsGOSE score alone is not significantly associated with QOL. Estimated marginal trends showed that higher GOSE scores were strongly associated with better QOL in the Independence (p < 0.001), Thinking (p < 0.001), and Physical (p = 0.019) domains. A weak, non-significant association was observed with the Feelings domain. No significant association was found between GOSE scores and the Social domain.ConclusionFunctional recovery after TBI is most closely related to independence, cognitive, and physical QOL but does not adequately reflect social or emotional well-being. These psychosocial domains may require targeted intervention and further emphasizes the importance of incorporating patient-reported QOL measures to more holistically assess recovery.

piezas.titulo: From a surgeon's stroke to a third hemisphere—The auxilium architecture for brain restoration and extension
piezas.resumenOriginal: A surgeon was exercising on a stationary bicycle when he had a large ischemic left middle cerebral artery territory stroke, complicated by hemorrhagic transformation requiring hemicraniectomy and cranioplasty. He developed right-sided spastic hemiplegia and a mixed aphasia. This paper takes that case as its anchor to pose the question: beyond improving residual function, what would it mean to restore cognitive function that was lost so that the person fully returns to their pre-stroke baseline? Existing brain-computer interfaces rely on the person having an intact cortical substrate for intended movement and speech. Here we propose the Auxilium, a brain restoration architecture for the situation where that substrate is no longer present: an extracranial auxiliary brain system, agnostic to its substrate, that connects to a person's residual cortex through whatever input-output technology proves most appropriate, and that supplies, in parallel and in real time, new substrate, whether biological or synthetic. We address an assumption of brain-computer interface development, that throughput is the binding constraint. Linking a kHz brain to MHz digital does not impart the higher clock speed, because the limitation lies not in the port but in the architecture of the entire brain and body imparted by evolution. We posit that the substrate of canonical circuits and their integration areas is essential, and the Auxilium can be understood as restoring both connectivity (linkage between disconnected areas) and computation (information generation capability of a volume of neural tissue). We propose a near-term de-risking pipeline using stereoelectroencephalography during surgical epilepsy evaluation, comparing extracranial modules spanning threshold rules, PID controllers, expert systems, artificial neural networks, neuromorphic devices, and biological specimens, each linked in real time to a participant serving as their own control on naturalistic tasks. If ports alone restore the lost function, the requirement is routing connectivity. If performance improves only when the module supplies its own dynamics, the requirement is computational substrate. We expect the answer to depend on how much tissue was lost, how quickly, and on the individual's reserve, and we treat routing and substrate as endpoints of a continuum to be mapped empirically.

piezas.titulo: A clinically identified Kirrel3 variant disrupts trans-synaptic circuit assembly
piezas.resumenOriginal: Trans-synaptic adhesion molecules guide selective connections between neurons to establish circuit specificity. Yet, there are gaps in the understanding of how many synaptic adhesion molecules function in vivo and if clinically identified variants perturb their function. Using cell-type-specific deletion in the mouse hippocampus, we show that Kirrel3 is required in both pre-synaptic DG neurons and post-synaptic GABA neurons to form DG-to-GABA excitatory synapses that drive a feed-forward inhibitory connection to CA3. These data provide in vivo, genetic evidence for a homophilic trans-synaptic Kirrel3 interaction driving synapse formation. Moderately increasing or decreasing wildtype Kirrel3 expression did not detectably alter synapse formation or CA3 neuron activity. In contrast, expression of a Kirrel3 missense variant identified in an individual with autism dominantly disrupts synapse formation and CA3 activity in vivo, providing a mechanism by which a single missense allele could disrupt circuit assembly and contribute to disease.

fuente.nota: Ya estaba en el proyecto antes de este catalogo. Preprints sin revision por pares.

destilado.texto: ¿Puede una sola mutación alterar la arquitectura cerebral? Un estudio de bioRxiv muestra que el gen Kirrel3 es esencial para que neuronas dentadas y GABA formen sinapsis excitadoras que regulan la actividad en CA3. La variante missense asociada al autismo interrumpe esa unión y reduce la señal en CA3, lo que sugiere un posible vínculo con la enfermedad.

piezas.titulo: Determinants of MoCA improvement in post-ischemic stroke patients receiving acupuncture: a retrospective study
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundAcupuncture is commonly integrated into multimodal rehabilitation programs for post-ischemic stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI), but the factors associated with cognitive improvement in this complex treatment context remain unclear. This retrospective study investigated factors associated with cognitive improvement in stroke patients receiving acupuncture as part of a standardized multimodal inpatient rehabilitation program.MethodsIn this single-center retrospective cohort study, 226 ischemic stroke patients treated with acupuncture between January 2023 and December 2025 were enrolled. Demographic data, clinical characteristics, acupuncture treatment parameters, and laboratory indicators were collected from electronic medical records. Cognitive function was assessed using MoCA, MMSE, LOTCA, MBI, HAMD, HAMA, and PSQI scales. Patients were categorized into improvement (ΔMoCA ≥2) and non-improvement groups. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were used to identify factors associated with cognitive improvement.ResultsAmong the 226 patients, 148 (65.49%) achieved improvement. After treatment, the improvement group showed significant improvements in MoCA and MMSE scores compared with baseline and the non-improvement group [between-group difference for post-treatment MoCA: 1.59 (95% CI 0.82 to 2.36; p < 0.001); MMSE: 2.44 (95% CI 1.69 to 3.19; p < 0.001)]. Significant improvements were also observed in LOTCA, MBI, HAMD, HAMA, and PSQI scores in the improvement group (p < 0.001). Univariate analysis identified age, education years, admission NIHSS score, diabetes mellitus, time to acupuncture intervention, treatment frequency, and total treatment course as factors associated with recovery (p < 0.05). Multivariate analysis demonstrated that advanced age (OR = 1.208, p < 0.001), higher NIHSS score (OR = 1.643, p = 0.001), longer time from stroke onset to acupuncture intervention (OR = 1.162, p = 0.011) and diabetes mellitus (OR = 4.737, p = 0.018) were associated with a lower probability of achieving the ΔMoCA improvement threshold. In contrast, longer education duration (OR = 0.740, p = 0.006), higher treatment frequency (OR = 0.271, p < 0.001), and longer treatment course (OR = 0.248, p < 0.001) were associated with a higher probability of meeting the improvement threshold. However, as treatment frequency and total course were determined during the clinical course rather than at baseline, these associations should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating, and do not imply causality.ConclusionIn this retrospective cohort of PSCI patients receiving acupuncture within a multimodal inpatient rehabilitation setting, shorter time from stroke onset to acupuncture initiation, higher weekly frequency, and longer treatment duration were exploratory factors associated with a greater likelihood of meeting the predefined ΔMoCA improvement threshold in this cohort. These hypothesis-generating observations may inform the design of future prospective studies and suggest patient characteristics that warrant further investigation. However, given the uncontrolled design, these findings cannot establish acupuncture-specific efficacy and should be considered hypothesis-generating, warranting confirmation through prospective randomized controlled trials.

destilado.texto: La mejora cognitiva tras un ictus isquémico se asocia a la acupuntura integrada en rehabilitación. piezas.titulo: LEGaTO: Low-Energy Heterogeneous Computing Workshop
piezas.resumenOriginal: Workshops Friday, 04 September, 2020 LEGaTO is a three-year H2020 project on developing a toolset for low-energy heterogeneous computing that also considers fault tolerance, programmability and security. The project optimized a number of use cases for low-energy. The objective of the workshop is to apply the optimization low-energy techniques to other stakeholders in each of the project's use cases. Scope We are broadly looking to engage the Artificial Intelligence, Smart City, Smart Home, Helthcare and IOT communities to evangalize the low-energy optimization techniques that we have developed for these communities during the lifetime of the LEGaTO project. In particular, we will showcase how the heterogeneous low-energy small form-factor hardware could be coupled to an energy efficient runtime to produce one order of energy savings across these use cases. The workshop will consist of invited talks from these communities and will include insights gained during the project for ensuring fault-tolerance and security in addition to energy efficiency. Tentative programme Friday 4 September 2020 (CEST) 9.45-10.00 Opening remarks and LEGATO Introduction 10.00-10.30 Keynote talk 10.30-11.15 Session 1: Energy Efficiency Abstract: Information and Communication Technology (ICT) is forecasted to global electricity usage by 2030 was estimated at 21% in a likely scenario and 51% in the worst-case. This bleak outlook requires the ICT sector to take urgent and radical action to limit the energy consumption of the sector. This session will look at unconventional means to achieve this goal. All market segments of the ICT area from Supercomputers to Embedded HPC systems will need to be radically energy-efficient; these two cases will be highlighted in the session. 11.15-11.30 Comfort break 11.30-12.15 Session 2: Fault Tolerance and Security Abstract: With the scaling of technology node to 6-7 nanometers, transistors are becoming more susceptible to transient and permanent errors. On the other hand, security lapses are making it very challenging to patch hardware/software of ICT systems. This session will look into fault-tolerance and security challenges facing datacenters and embedded systems. 12.15-13.00 Session 3: AI and Smart City / Smart Home Abstract: The proliferation of edge and fog computing and the availability of data generated by zero emissions electric vehicles and smart home automation have driven the ICT industry to provide AI-driven solutions for these use cases. In this session we will discuss the convergence of HPC and AI in smart city/home market segments. 13.00-14.00 Lunch break 14.00-14.45 Session 4: FPGAs and Programming Models Abstract: FPGAs have become an attractive compute fabric which offers almost ASIC class performance per watt. However, their progammability had been an issue that impacted their take-up by more use cases. Recently, FPGAs have become easier to program as well as providing leadership class performance per watt. This sesssion will discuss recent FPGA developments in energy-efficiency and programmability. 14.45-15.30 Closed poster session (LEGaTO students) 15.30-15.45 Comfort break 15.45-16.30 Session 5: EU related projects 16.30-17.00 Wrap-up and conclusions Online Registration Free No heterogeneous https://legato-project.eu/event/legato-low-energy-heterogeneous-computing-workshop More information This workshop will analize the low-energy optimization techniques that have been developed by the LEGaTO project for the Artificial Intelligence, Smart City, Smart Home, Healthcare and IOT communities.

piezas.titulo: State-dependent responses of emotional brain networks in high myopia under blurred vision: a shift towards dorsal stream and cross-modal processing
piezas.resumenOriginal: PurposeReliable sensory input plays a vital role in shaping emotional experience, however, how the brain modulates the formation of emotion under chronic visual degradation remains unclear. Using high myopia (HM) as a natural model of sustained blur, this study investigated state-dependent responses of emotional brain networks during blurred movie viewing.MethodsTwenty-four participants with high myopia (HM) were tested without optical correction, comparing with normal vision (NV) controls from previous research. All participants watched thriller and scenic movie clips twice over one week during fMRI. Intra-subject synchrony and seed-based functional connectivity analyses focused on the amygdala and visual processing streams.ResultsCompared to NV controls, the HM group exhibited reduced intra-subject synchrony in visual cortices but increased synchrony in the primary auditory cortex, indicating cross-modal compensatory enhancement. During threat processing, HM participants showed strengthened and stable functional connectivity between the amygdala and the dorsal visual stream. For non-threatening content, this enhanced connectivity initially involved both dorsal and ventral stream but persisted selectively in the dorsal stream upon repeated viewing.ConclusionSustained visual blur elicits a perceptual-state-dependent functional response in emotional networks, characterized by heightened cross-modal auditory integration and an increased recruitment of the visual dorsal stream during blurred viewing. These findings highlight the brain’s immediate compensatory mechanisms under conditions of ambiguous visual input.

destilado.texto: La visión borrosa reduce la sincronía visual y aumenta la auditiva en sujetos con alto miopía. El estudio, publicado por Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, mostró que el amígdala se conecta más con la vía dorsal visual durante escenas amenazantes. ¿Podrá esta compensación auditiva mejorar la percepción emocional?

piezas.titulo: From micro-architecture to networks: canonical neurobiological architecture of functional brain organization across the lifespan and in psychopathology
piezas.resumenOriginal: Understanding how macroscale functional network connectivity (FNC) across the lifespan and in psychopathology is spatially organized with respect to microscale neurobiological architecture remains a challenge. Here, we constructed a cross-omics mapping framework by linking resting-state fMRI data (5,349 individuals, 6-80 years) with 49 neurobiological markers (24 cell types, 19 neurotransmitters, 6 mitochondria). We show that FNC development and aging unfold along cellular and molecular gradients. Specifically, spatial correspondence between age-related FNC changes and neurobiological microprofile networks varied by life stage, peaking for cell types in adolescence, neurotransmitter systems in mid-young adulthood and mitochondrial phenotypes in early adulthood. Applying normative modeling to 5 psychiatric disorders (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, autism, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), we identified disorder-specific and cross-disorder FNC phenotypes spatially associated with neurobiological architecture. Together, these findings provide a hypothesis-generating framework linking functional brain organization and dysfunction to canonical neurobiological architecture across the lifespan and psychiatric disorders.

piezas.titulo: MicroWorld: Empowering Multimodal Large Language Models to Bridge the Microscopic Domain Gap with Multimodal Attributed Property Graph
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2605.10120v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show remarkable potential for scientific reasoning, yet their performance in specialized domains such as microscopy remains limited by the scarcity of domain-specific training data and the difficulty of encoding fine-grained expert knowledge into model parameters. To bridge the gap, we introduce MicroWorld, a framework for structured-knowledge augmentation with a complementary visual retrieval pathway, using a multimodal attributed property graph (MAPG) without domain-specific fine-tuning. MicroWorld extracts biomedical entities and relations via scispaCy or LLM-based triplet mining, aligns images and entities in a shared embedding space using Qwen3-VL-Embedding, and assembles a knowledge graph comprising approximately 106K nodes and 2.62M typed edges spanning eight relation categories. At inference time, a graph-augmented retrieval pipeline matches query entities to the MAPG and injects structured knowledge context into the MLLM prompt. On MicroVQA, MicroWorld raises Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct accuracy from 48.8% to 67.1% (+18.3 percentage points; 37.5% relative), exceeding zero-shot GPT-5 (59.4%). The identical retrieved context raises GPT-5 to 71.5%, and GPT-5's own entity extraction reaches 73.3%. On MicroBench, 8B Single-Pass improves overall accuracy by 4.0 percentage points. The benefits are greatest for knowledge-intensive reasoning; fine-grained visual discrimination and the additional visual-pathway contribution remain limited. Code and accompanying resources: https://github.com/ieellee/MicroWorld.

destilado.texto: No es solo cuestión de capacidad de razonamiento: también de acceso a datos microscópicos. piezas.titulo: Application of weighted gene co-expression network analysis to explore the targets of treadmill training in rats with spinal cord injury
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundSpinal cord injury (SCI) describes any damage to the spinal cord that results in a loss of function. With these injuries being commonly treated with subsequent treadmill training (TM), this study aimed to reveal the mechanisms facilitating TM-mediated rehabilitation following a SCI.MethodsDifferentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified and then subjected to a weighted gene co-expression network analysis to identify TM-associated modules. Co-expression network construction, functional annotation, protein–protein interaction (PPI) network, and transcription factor (TF)-miRNA-target regulatory network were then conducted. We established an SCI rat model and validated key RNAs using reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). Predicted interactions between miR-135a-5p and JAK2 and STAT1 were tested using dual-luciferase reporter assay.ResultsTotal 640 and 877 genes separately differentially expressed in SCI 8d + TM vs. SCI 8d and SCI 14d + TM vs. SCI 14d comparison groups were screened and merged as the DEGs, which were further narrowed to four TM-associated modules linked to the glutamatergic synapse and ribosome biogenesis pathways. PPI network evaluations identified v-Akt murine thymoma viral oncogene homolog 1 (AKT1), Janus kinase 2 (JAK2), tumor necrosis factor (TNF), and signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1) as hub nodes. JAK2 and STAT1 were also shown to have interactions in module b. TF-miRNA-target regulatory network revealed that both STAT1 and JAK2 were targets of miR-135a. RT-qPCR results confirmed upregulation of AKT1 and STAT1 and downregulation of JAK2, TNF and miR-135a after TM. Dual-luciferase reporter assays revealed the direct binding of miR-135a-5p to JAK2 and STAT1.ConclusionThese findings suggest that TM facilitates SCI recovery by regulating AKT1, JAK2, TNF, STAT1 and miR-135a.

piezas.titulo: Accordion: Elastic-Depth Inference via Fixed-Prefix Layer Looping
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2610.32492v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models serve applications with diverse inference budgets, but training and maintaining separate models for each budget incurs substantial costs. Recent Looped Transformers enable flexible inference computation through parameter reuse, but maintaining strong performance across different inference budgets remains an open challenge. We introduce Accordion, a mixture-of-experts-based model that supports five inference budgets through fixed-prefix layer looping. Each budget follows a pre-defined execution path, while the minimum budget retains the unlooped model. Joint pretraining samples one budget per micro-batch and optimizes its next-token prediction loss without additional cross-budget consistency objectives. We further preserve these inference budgets through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, where parameter-group merging and budget-matched multi-teacher on-policy distillation integrate three domain experts into one model. After 3.6T tokens of pretraining, increasing inference depth improves Accordion-6B-A0.5B's five-category macro-average across 37 tasks by 3.01 percentage points, with the middle budget capturing 89% of this gain using half as many additional layer executions. The final model surpasses each domain expert on its corresponding task-and-budget average, while achieving strong instruction-following performance across all budgets and retaining depth-dependent gains in mathematical reasoning and code generation.

piezas.titulo: SpecAgent: Empowering Program Verification with Agentic Synthesis of Formal Program Specifications
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2610.05132v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Formal specifications are essential for deductive program verification, providing semantic abstractions for compositional verification of complex software. However, manually constructing specifications is labor-intensive, motivating automated synthesis. Despite recent advances in large language models (LLMs), existing approaches often rely on forward-only workflows and localized repair, limiting their effectiveness on real-world programs with complex dependencies among functions and loops. Verification failures may stem from previously generated specifications, causing cascading failures that local refinement cannot resolve. To address these challenges, we present SpecAgent, an agentic framework for synthesizing high-quality ACSL specifications for real-world C programs. SpecAgent integrates four components: dependency-aware planning to identify specification targets, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to provide relevant specification patterns and program context, agentic repair to diagnose defects and revisit dependent specifications, and agentic critique to assess and refine semantic strength beyond proof success. We evaluate SpecAgent on specification synthesis and program verification tasks. On 50 programs from 14 real-world repositories, SpecAgent with DeepSeek-V4 achieves 96.82% precision and 88.95% recall in synthesizing correct and strong specifications, outperforming all baselines. On 811 real-world verification targets, it successfully discharges 604, also surpassing existing baselines. These results demonstrate SpecAgent's effectiveness in synthesizing high-quality specifications and facilitating real-world program verification.

fuente.nota: Ya estaba en el proyecto antes de este catalogo. Preprints sin revision por pares.

destilado.texto: Generar especificaciones formales automáticamente reduce la carga manual en la verificación de programas. SpecAgent integra planificación dependiente, generación aumentada por recuperación, reparación agente y crítica agente para crear especificaciones ACSL robustas. Su éxito sugiere que equipos podrían acelerar la validación de código sin depender de ajustes costosos.

piezas.titulo: Fragments: September 16
piezas.resumenOriginal: Reports of agentic hacking continue, in this case it happened back in May and it seems OpenAI did not disclose that they were responsible. Simon Willison sees two options: After the Hugging Face and Wiki attacks OpenAI were still unable to review their previous logs and determine that they had previously attacked RubyGems. They knew about the attack on RubyGems and made the decision not to reach out to the RubyGems team about it. Both of these are bad! Given this incident, the Hugging Face situation, and the Wiki attack, the obvious question right now is how many more incidents like this are out there waiting to be discovered? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Dave Farley: Stop asking the sci-fi question: ‘Is it conscious?’ Start asking the engineering question: ‘Is this a powerful, unpredictable component being put somewhere consequential, and where’s the feedback that tells us that it’s safe? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Nate Silver is known for his forecasts, but to do them he writes a lot of code for his models. He’s found agentic engineering capable of doing miraculous work . In spending so much time with the LLMs, I’m super attentive to improvements in their capabilities. And these changes tend not to be so linear. Instead, they improve in step functions, almost as phase changes. Suddenly, the models just start doing things capably that they were screwing up before. In my experience, there was a big leap forward when reasoning models first came out in late 2024/early 2025 — enough that they were occasionally useful for tasks involving data and not just words — and then another one this past winter. The most recent changes I’ve noticed, however, have had less to do with intelligence and more with persistence. Consider the Hugging Face attack. Although these agents showed remarkable intelligence, they weren’t really super-intelligent - but they were super-persistent. This is a common theme of AI in its various forms: Game engines like AlphaGo Zero start out by basically making random moves — but by playing against themselves millions of times, they eventually far surpass human capabilities As we try to figure out what kind of regulations we need to keep AI under control, we need to remember that we should design our guards around super-persistence as much as worrying about super-intelligence. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ “Uncle Bob” Martin has made many posts on X during the last few months about his programming with LLMs. His approach has been to build a firm harness to keep them under control, so they create software that is maintainable as well as functional. Sadly the posts have been frustratingly light on detail. But now it seems that lack of information may not matter And while I was heads-down getting that to work, the agents got a LOT better. So much so that when I came up for air, the need for my harness was obviated. Indeed, the need for any but the most liberal of harnesses may be obviated. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Some tidbits that struck me from Ezra Klein’s recent (recommended) interview with Matt Sheehan on the interplay between regulation of AI and competition with China . While Chinese models have made some surprisingly remarkable gains in the slipstream of US frontier models, the US still has 8 times as much compute available to it than China - which is a material gap. People in the US worry that regulation will slow down the US model builders, but these rapid recent gains in China have occurred under much more regulation Americans say that when they set up a hotline to talk to Chinese leaders in a crisis, the Chinese don’t pick up the phone. But this misunderstands the Chinese system. Individual Chinese, even powerful ones, aren’t given individual decision-making power. They operate with committees and documents. So the Americans are better off sending a fax than trying to call an individual Like so many things, effective regulation needs regular practice When American policymakers are like: Where do you start? — I sometimes say: Well, you start by starting. You learn how to regulate things, you learn how to legislate on them by regulating and legislating on them.

destilado.texto: Los reportes de hacking agente continúan y parece que OpenAI ocultó su responsabilidad. piezas.titulo: Blood flow restriction training for lower-limb function, walking and functional recovery after stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundBlood flow restriction training (BFRT) is increasingly used as a low-load rehabilitation strategy after stroke, but the magnitude, clinical relevance, and certainty of its effects remain uncertain. We evaluated the effects and safety of BFRT on lower-limb function and mobility after stroke.MethodsPubMed, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, CENTRAL, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, and SinoMed were searched from inception to June 10, 2026. Randomized controlled trials evaluating lower-limb BFRT in adults after stroke were included. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2, certainty using GRADE, and random-effects meta-analyses were performed.ResultsNineteen randomized controlled trials were included. BFRT improved Fugl-Meyer Assessment of the Lower Extremity scores (10 studies, 646 participants; MD = 2.14 points, 95% CI 0.74 to 3.54) and Berg Balance Scale scores (8 studies, 581 participants; MD = 4.72 points, 95% CI 1.62 to 7.82). The 10-meter walk test analysis showed higher walking speed (4 studies, 322 participants; MD = 0.14 m/s, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.25), but the estimate attenuated after eligible grey literature was included (6 studies, 410 participants; MD = 0.09 m/s, 95% CI − 0.03 to 0.21). Six-minute walk distance increased by 8.01 m (5 studies, 271 participants; 95% CI 2.31 to 13.71). No clear pooled effects were observed for Timed Up and Go, sit-to-stand performance, cadence, or standard full-scale Barthel Index/Modified Barthel Index scores. FMA-LE and 6MWT effects were below reported clinically important thresholds; the BBS estimate was close to an approximately 5-point reference, with its confidence interval spanning effects below and above that threshold. Certainty was moderate for 6MWT, low for FMA-LE, and very low for BBS and 10MWT walking speed. No BFRT-related serious adverse or thrombotic events were reported among studies with explicit safety information, although reporting was limited.ConclusionBFRT may improve selected lower-limb outcomes after stroke, but clinical importance remains uncertain for several outcomes and certainty ranges from moderate to very low.
